abstract: The New York Fed's third annual read on AI in its regional business surveys, and the first where a majority of firms on both sides of the survey report using AI. Among firms in New York State and northern New Jersey, 61% of service firms reported using AI as part of their business processes in August 2026, up from 40% in 2025 and 25% in 2024. Manufacturers went from 16% to 26% to 51% over the same three years. The authors' argument is that this adoption is wide but shallow, and that it is showing up in how work is organized rather than in headcount. Three-quarters of service firms and more than 90% of manufacturers describe their AI investment as minimal to modest, and among adopters the median firm reports only 17% of its workers (services) or 7% (manufacturing) actually using the technology. On the labor side, 4% of service adopters reported laying off workers because of AI, 15% said they hired fewer workers than they otherwise would have, and 13% said they hired more — while just over a third of service firms and more than 20% of manufacturers report retraining workers. The retraining share exceeds every displacement channel they measure, which is the basis for the title. Regional and self-reported, so it is not comparable to the national Census BTOS series, but it is one of the few sources that measures firm adoption and within-firm worker uptake in the same instrument.
keyFindings: Service-firm AI use reached 61% in August 2026, up from 40% in 2025 and 25% in 2024; manufacturers reached 51%, roughly double the 26% in 2025 and triple the 16% in 2024.

AI users are defined as firms using the technology 'as part of their business processes,' explicitly excluding firms using AI only as an information search tool — a stricter bar than most adoption surveys.

Adoption is shallow: three-quarters of service firms and more than 90% of manufacturers characterize their AI investments as minimal to modest; only 15% of service firms report significant resource commitments and about 5% treat AI as a major strategic investment.
Among adopters, the median firm reports just 17% of its workers using AI in services and 7% in manufacturing — firm-level adoption substantially overstates worker-level use.
Only 4% of service adopters reported laying off workers because of AI, up from 1% in 2025; no manufacturers reported AI-related layoffs.
Hiring effects roughly offset: about 15% of service firms hired fewer workers than they otherwise would have because of AI, and about 13% hired more.
Retraining is the dominant response: just over a third of service firms and more than 20% of manufacturers report retraining workers, exceeding every displacement channel measured.

Among non-adopters, roughly half say their work is unsuitable for AI and about a quarter say AI is not yet capable enough; data privacy/security, accuracy/reliability, and lack of technical staff are each cited by about a third.
methodology: Analysis of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's regional business surveys — the Empire State Manufacturing Survey and the Business Leaders Survey of regional service firms — which have carried a supplemental AI module each August since 2024. Coverage is New York State and northern New Jersey (the Second District), not the nation. Adoption is measured by asking whether the firm uses AI as part of its business processes, with firms using AI exclusively as an information search tool coded as non-users. Workforce questions ask adopters about layoffs, hiring changes, and retraining attributable to AI over the prior six months. Worker uptake is captured as each adopting firm's reported share of its own workers using AI, reported as a median across firms. Authors: Jaison R. Abel, Richard Deitz, Natalia Emanuel, and Nick Montalbano.
qualifiers: Regional, not national: the Second District skews toward finance, professional services, and information relative to the US economy, so the 61%/51% adoption levels should not be set against the national Census BTOS figure (about 22% in mid-2026), which also uses a two-week rather than six-month reference window and a different definition of use. All measures are firm self-report with no payroll validation, and firms are asked to attribute hiring and layoff decisions to AI specifically — a firm that slowed hiring for several reasons at once need not name AI. The workforce questions are asked only of adopters, so the shares are of AI-using firms rather than of all firms or all workers. The median-share-of-workers figure is a median across firms, not a share of regional employment, and cannot be read as a worker-level adoption rate. The 4% layoff figure rises from a 1% base, so the proportional jump rests on very small counts. The authors state plainly that AI technology and its applications are still evolving rapidly and that these patterns could shift as adoption matures.
